- When sentiment is consistently negative (e.g., 0.00 or -0.33) over recent days, model tends to overcorrect upward — reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >5% from prior day), model often overshoots and fails to correct — apply downward drag or lagged mean reversion to prevent overextension.
- In high-event periods (e.g., >15 events/30d, net supply negative), model underestimates downside risk — increase downward bias or add volatility penalty to forecast.
- If sentiment is bullish but price declines sharply (e.g., >3% drop from prior day), model often fails to adjust — add a “bearish sentiment override” if sentiment drops below 0.50.
- Model tends to ignore sentiment shifts in early days of event window — require sentiment history to be weighted more heavily in first 5–7 days of forecast horizon.
- In multi-event weeks (e.g., 3+ auctions in 7 days), model often underestimates cumulative supply shock — add supply net adjustment to forecast baseline.
- If sentiment is mixed (e.g., 0.67–1.00) and price is trending down, model often fails to recognize reversal — apply “sentiment decay” rule: if sentiment drops below 0.50, reduce forecast slope by 10–20%.
- Model often overestimates mean reversion in low-event periods — in low-event windows, allow forecast to drift with sentiment, not revert to prior mean.
